Description
I assume running a function one single time is sufficient to jit-compile it. However, I came across a situation where the jit compilation might require an arbitrary number of function runs.
Here is a snippet that showcases this behavior where:

I create a function to be jit-compiled (the function is for the sake of illustration)
I run it and time its execution for several input sizes


(click to expend code snippet)
import time
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp


# A dummy function
@jax.jit
def some_func(vec, indices):
    out = jnp.zeros(len(indices))

    for idx, j in enumerate(indices):
        out_j = vec[j]
        out = out.at[idx].set(out_j)

    return out


timings = []
x = jnp.ones(20)

for n_indices in [5, 8, 10, 10, 10]:
    # make a list of indices
    li = jnp.arange(n_indices)

    # time the execution of function
    start = time.perf_counter()
    some_func(x, li)
    end = time.perf_counter()

    timings.append(end - start)

Plotting the timings gives the following figure.
One can observe that:

The jit compilation process was executed 3 times
The last two runs (with the same input size) didn't trigger any compilation


I'm pretty confused about the origin of this behavior: I can't tell whether it is a bug or an inherent functioning of Jax.
My concern is that jit compilation comes with a time overhead which would be amplified if it requires many function runs.

  assert x.dtype == jnp.float64

nodes.bodyText: In order to run JAX programs with custom calls on other compiler/runtime backends (eg. OpenXLA/IREE), the custom call implementations have to be registered with the backend. PJRT is meant to be the shim-layer between frontends like JAX and backends like XLA and OpenXLA. Right now custom calls are registered only on the XLA backend using xla_client.register_custom_call_target. It would be ideal to create a new register_custom_call_target in the PJRT API and allow the PJRT clients (such as https://github.com/openxla/openxla-pjrt-plugin) to implement the registration. JAX calls pjrt.register_custom_call_target to register the custom call implementations.

Hi, thank you for your work 🙂,  I am interested in coding ensemble neural networks in JAX / Flax. I tried to vmap over the individual networks to make the overall forward pass faster. It seems that it is lower than doing a for loop over each individual network. Shouldn't it be the opposite?
I also tried to use scan instead of vmap or a for loop and I get similar performances than the for loop.
The way I code the ensemble network is by coding one MLP and then generating as much parameters as I want individual networks.
Here is the code, you can run it on Google colab here:
from functools import partial
from time import time

from typing import Sequence
import flax.linen as nn
from flax.core import FrozenDict
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp


class MLP(nn.Module):
  features: Sequence[int]

  @nn.compact
  def __call__(self, x):
    for feat in self.features[:-1]:
      x = nn.relu(nn.Dense(feat)(x))
    x = nn.Dense(self.features[-1])(x)
    return x


class MultiMLPNet:
    def __init__(self, n_mlps: int, features: Sequence) -> None:
        self.n_mlps = n_mlps
        self.features = features
        self.mlp = MLP(self.features)

    @partial(jax.jit, static_argnames="self")
    def init_vmap(self, key: jax.random.PRNGKey, x: jnp.ndarray) -> FrozenDict:
        return jax.vmap(self.mlp.init, in_axes=[0, None])(jax.random.split(key, self.n_mlps), x)

    @partial(jax.jit, static_argnames="self")
    def apply_vmap(self, params: FrozenDict, x: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
        return jax.vmap(self.mlp.apply, in_axes=[0, None])(params, x)
    
    @partial(jax.jit, static_argnames="self")
    def init_loop(self, key: jax.random.PRNGKey, x: jnp.ndarray) -> FrozenDict:
        params = {}

        for idx_mlp in range(self.n_mlps):
            key, _ = jax.random.split(key)
            params[f"mlp_{idx_mlp}"] = self.mlp.init(key, x)

        return FrozenDict(**params)
    
    @partial(jax.jit, static_argnames="self")
    def apply_loop(self, params: FrozenDict, x: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
        output = jnp.zeros((self.n_mlps, self.features[-1]))

        for idx_mlp in range(self.n_mlps):
            output = output.at[idx_mlp].set(self.mlp.apply(params[f"mlp_{idx_mlp}"], x))

        return output

    @partial(jax.jit, static_argnames="self")
    def apply_scan(self, params: FrozenDict, x: jnp.ndarray) -> jnp.ndarray:
        def f(carry, params_idx_mlp): 
            return None, multi_mlp_net.mlp.apply(params_idx_mlp, x)

        return jax.lax.scan(f, None, params)[1]

params_loop = multi_mlp_net.init_loop(jax.random.PRNGKey(0), x)
multi_mlp_net.apply_loop(params_loop, x)

Hello,
After discussion  #15204
Here is a code to deal with the convolution using FFT of two 2D real arrays. It is mostly inspired from the scipy.fftconvolvefunction.  One use-case & test of this function is available on Colab  HERE with the JAX 0.4.6 version (this is the current one at least today). For sure my code is not the best one. Feel free to improve it.

I do nit know if the second array in2 can be smaller in size than the first one
for sure the complex-complex case would need some adaptation
finally the next_fast_len available in scipy  would improve the computation of the "good" FFT size.

@jax.jit
def convolve2r(in1,in2):

  # suppose
  # in1 = jnp.asarray(x1)
  # in2 = jnp.asarray(x2)
  #  "assert" in1.ndim == in2.ndim == 2
  #  "assert" in1.size == in2.size
  #  "assert" in1.dtype.kind == 'f' and in2.dtype.kind == "f"

  axes = range(in1.ndim)

  s1 = in1.shape
  s2 = in2.shape
  shape = [s1[i] + s2[i] -1 for i in range(in1.ndim)]
  
  # crude next_fast_len equivalent with just power of 2
  fshape = 2**np.ceil(np.log2(np.array(shape))).astype('uint16')

  fslice = tuple([slice(sz) for sz in shape])

  sp1 = jnp.fft.fftn(in1, fshape, axes=axes)
  sp2 = jnp.fft.fftn(in2, fshape, axes=axes)
  conv = jnp.fft.irfftn(sp1 * sp2, fshape, axes=axes)
  conv = conv[tuple(map(slice, shape))]   #conv = jax.lax.slice(conv,(0,0),(shape))

  def _centered(arr, newshape):
    # Return the center newshape portion of the array.
    newshape = np.asarray(newshape)
    currshape = np.array(arr.shape)
    startind = (currshape - newshape) // 2
    endind = startind + newshape
    myslice = [slice(startind[k], endind[k]) for k in range(len(endind))]
    return arr[tuple(myslice)]

  return _centered(conv, s1)

np.asarray(jax.Array()) requires being fully replicated OR being fully_addressable, but I think it's not the correct required condition. The required condition is: The local shards of the host should cover all the data of the jax.Array.
For example, here a dummy example, with 2 hosts, {TPU_0 and TPU_1} and {TPU_2, TPU_3}. If we imagine that the Array is sharded over the columns and that it's replicated over the rows, both host can reconstruct the jax.Array, but the jax.Array is not fully replicated  and it's also not fully addressable.

 │                                         │
 │ TPU_0          TPU_1       │
 │                                         │
 └──────────────┘
 ┌─────────────┐
 │                                      │

Description
I ran into this problem trying to register a custom operation (implemented in C++) that only returns a single output.
Mockup code for the jax side:
from functools import partial

import jax
from jax.interpreters import xla, mlir
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jax.lib import xla_client

from jax._src.abstract_arrays import ShapedArray

from jaxlib.hlo_helpers import custom_call
from jax.interpreters import mlir

import jax.numpy as jnp

# xla_client.register_cpu_custom_call_target(
#     b"single_return_fun_native", None # here register the actual native function capsule
# )

test_p = jax.core.Primitive("single_return_fun")
test_p.multiple_results = False
test_p.def_impl(partial(xla.apply_primitive, test_p))

def _abstract_eval(x):
    return ShapedArray(x.shape, x.dtype)

test_p.def_abstract_eval(_abstract_eval)


def _lowering(ctx, x):
    x_type = mlir.ir.RankedTensorType(x.type)
    x_shape = x_type.shape
    layout = range(len(x_shape) - 1, -1, -1)

    return custom_call(b"single_return_fun_native", out_types=[x_type], operands=[x], operand_layouts=[layout], result_layouts=[layout])

mlir.register_lowering(test_p, _lowering)


def single_return_fun(x):
    return test_p.bind(x)

x = jnp.zeros((3, 2))
single_return_fun(x)
The above fails with a ValueError with message
Output of translation rule must be iterable: a:f32[3,2] = single_return_fun b, got output Value(%0 = "stablehlo.custom_call"(%arg0) {api_version = 2 : i32, backend_config = "", call_target_name = "single_return_fun_native", called_computations = [], has_side_effect = false, operand_layouts = [dense<[1, 0]> : tensor<2xindex>], output_operand_aliases = [], result_layouts = [dense<[1, 0]> : tensor<2xindex>]} : (tensor<3x2xf32>) -> tensor<3x2xf32>)
This is caused by the implementation in hlo_helpers.custom_call , which returns a OpResult instance if only a single output is specified in the lowering rule, i.e., the length of out_types is one. (If the length is larger than one, this function instead returns List[OpResult].)
This then leads to a crash somewhere upstream in the translation stack, i.e., in
jaxpr_subcomp, which expects to always get an iterable and will throw the above exception if this is not the case.
Note that the setting of test_p.multiple_results = False doesn't factor in here. The behaviour of custom_call is only dependent on the length its out_types argument, which is in turn determined by the native/C side implementation.
As a workaround, I tried to add an additional empty return value (i.e., an array of length 0), but that resulted in another error.
Making hlo_helpers.custom_call return a list containing a single element if len(out_types) == 1 fixes this error. (But in that case, the test above crashes because the custom call target single_return_fun_native has not actually been registered. I could not find a concise way of doing that for this bug report.)
